title: Why Inventing Color TV Was So Difficult

body:
in History, Media, Technology |   	September 4th, 2026  Leave a Comment
	
			

	

Many who read this will remem­ber watch­ing tele­vi­sion on a black-and-white set at some point in their lives. Few­er will remem­ber doing so because only black-and-white sets exist­ed. Of course, your own expe­ri­ence will depend upon your coun­try of ori­gin. The Unit­ed States began the tran­si­tion to col­or tele­vi­sion in 1953, and more than half of its pop­u­la­tion owned col­or sets less than twen­ty years there­after. France’s sta­tions start­ed to change over in 1967, and the last one did so in 1983. South Korea, where I live, start­ed its own reg­u­lar col­or broad­casts in 1980, though at that point, those from the Amer­i­can Forces Net­work, Japan, and even North Korea could already be tuned in for years.
Today we all take col­or TV for grant­ed, but as the Pri­mal Space video above explains, its inven­tion was no sim­ple mat­ter. Still, it occurred much ear­li­er than most of us would imag­ine. In 1925, Scot­tish inven­tor John Logie Baird came up with the first tele­vi­sion, which involved pass­ing light through holes in a spin­ning disc onto a pho­to­elec­tric cell for trans­mis­sion through cables or radio waves. This sys­tem could only reg­is­ter the bright­ness of the light, pro­duc­ing a black-and-white image. But the mech­a­nism itself sug­gest­ed a means of intro­duc­ing col­or: enlarge the disc, add sep­a­rate sets of holes for red, green, and blue, and repro­duce a frame of each in quick, cycli­cal suc­ces­sion at the oth­er end, tak­ing advan­tage of the human eye­’s ten­den­cy to col­lapse them into a sin­gle image.
Baird first demon­strat­ed his col­or tele­vi­sion sys­tem in 1928. Though impres­sive, it also looked unlike­ly to per­form at a scale that could pro­duce a sharp, smooth mov­ing pic­ture. Oth­er engi­neers saw more tele­vi­su­al promise in the tech­nol­o­gy of the cath­ode ray tube, or CRT, which Japan­ese inven­tor Ken­jiro Takayana­gi had already har­nessed for his own black-and-white mechan­i­cal tele­vi­sion in the year before. The key com­po­nent was the icono­scope invent­ed by Vladimir Zworykin in 1933. “Essen­tial­ly the world’s first video cam­era,” it employed an inter­nal elec­tron gun to “scan” a cap­tured image into a trans­mis­si­ble elec­tri­cal sig­nal. Still, the ques­tion remained: how to do it in col­or?
Enter the Radio Cor­po­ra­tion of Amer­i­ca, whose abbre­vi­at­ed name more than a few of us will remem­ber from our child­hood TV sets. Hav­ing devel­oped a video cam­era “that took the incom­ing light and fil­tered it through spe­cial prisms to sep­a­rate the red, green, and blue,” con­vert­ing each into its own sig­nal, RCA then faced the prob­lem of deliv­er­ing the result to view­ers at home. None of the more than five mil­lion black-and-white sets already extant in the U.S. could receive those three sig­nals at all. The solu­tion involved using one elec­tron gun per col­or, each of whose sig­nals would be encod­ed so as to be hid­den in the exist­ing black-and-white tele­vi­sion sig­nal and then decod­ed by col­or sets. Con­sumers may not have tak­en up the tech­nol­o­gy all at once, but those who did in time for The Wiz­ard of Oz’s first broad­cast in 1956 sure­ly under­stood that col­or TV had a future.
Relat­ed Con­tent:

Based in Seoul, Col­in Marshall writes and broad­casts on cities, lan­guage, and cul­ture. He’s the author of the newslet­ter Books on Cities as well as the books 한국 요약 금지 (No Sum­ma­riz­ing Korea) and Kore­an Newtro. Fol­low him on the social net­work for­mer­ly known as Twit­ter at @colinmarshall.

title: Go Behind the Scenes of Blackwing Pencils' Ode to Analog Creativity
description: Headquartered in Stockton, California, Blackwing is about finding the joy in analog creative tools at a time when digital devices consume our atte
body:
Headquartered in Stockton, California, Blackwing is about finding the joy in analog creative tools at a time when digital devices consume our attention. The manufacturer produces its signature pencils in a series of specialized factories in Japan, where the graphite cores are meticulously processed before being sent to a wood shop. In a behind-the-scenes video, the company shares how that process works, followed by how the utensils begin to take shape.
Sandwiched between slats of wood, individual pencils are then sliced and trimmed to their characteristic hexagonal shape. Yet another factory takes care of the painting and labeling, where depending on the style, the pencils can receive up to 10 coats of lacquer to achieve the final color and feel. And for the final step, the instruments journey to Stockton, where a proprietary machine attaches each eraser, and they’re inspected by hand before being boxed by the dozen.
Shop Blackwing in the Colossal Shop.

title: 'Inploration' Highlights Dozens of Artists Who Explore Space to Understand Earth
description: In his essay “The Passing Wisdom of Birds,” environmentalist and writer Barry Lopez rued how scientific methodology doesn’t take into consideratio
body:
In his essay “The Passing Wisdom of Birds,” environmentalist and writer Barry Lopez rued how scientific methodology doesn’t take into consideration our senses or perception, how data is divorced from the experience of nature. “Biology should borrow here from quantum physics, which accepts the premise that, under certain circumstances, the observer can be deceived,” he wrote. “Quantum physics, with its ambiguous particles and ten-dimensional universes, is a branch of science that has in fact returned us to a state of awe with nature, without threatening our intellectual capacity to analyze complex events.”
Such is the fascination that grounds the book Inploration: Art Exploring Space to Understand Earth, forthcoming from Delmonico Books. The volume is the result of years of work by Grammy award-winning creative director and curator Lawrence Azerrad and artist Richelle Ellis, who co-founded the platform Inploration. Ellis also founded Supercollider and has spent the past decade investigating what she describes as “the intersection of art and aerospace.” Both authors are drawn to the way our questioning of the universe can revive a sense of wonder for our planet and prompt us to consider how we value and care for it.
Cannupa Hanska Luger, “The One Who Checks & The One Who Balances” (2018 – ongoing), site-specific land acknowledgement, Navajo Nation. Photo by Chip Thomas, © 2024 Cannupa Hanska Luger
“We coined ‘inploration’ as a counterpart to exploration,” Ellis says. “Rather than looking outward in search of discovery, inploration turns inward, using our relationship to the greater cosmos as a way to better understand ourselves and the planet we inhabit.” The book compiles a wide range of studies, works of art, experiments, and insights from nearly 100 artists, scientists, astronauts, futurists, and others.
Colossal readers will recognize work by Cannupa Hanska Luger, Tavares Strachan, Wangechi Mutu, and more. From Cai Guo-Qiang’s 500-meter fiery ladder to James Turrell’s monumental earthwork in the Painted Desert with its skyward aperture, the book challenges us to think about our relationship to not only the earth but everything that exists in the incomprehensible beyond. The authors say:

Inploration is as much about charting a shift in perspective as it is about putting forward what this new vantage point means in terms of how we relate to our planet and our shared future. Throughout the ages, imagination and curiosity have driven the most consequential changes to how humanity understands and navigates across – and beyond – our planet. In the same manner, as we face the challenges and opportunities of a truly global culture, we aim to harness the power of wonder as something that is not naive, but absolutely necessary.

Inploration will be released at the end of October, and you can pre-order your copy on Bookshop.
Cai Guo-Qiang, “Sky Ladder” (2015), gunpowder, fuse and helium balloon, 500 x 5.5 meters (100 seconds). Realized at Huiyu Island Harbour, Quanzhou, Fujian, June 15, 2015, 4:45 am (dawn). Photo by Lin Yi, © Cai Studio
Lucy McRae, “Solitary Survival Raft” (2020). Photo by Ariel Fisher, © Lucy McRae
Azuma Makoto, “In Bloom #1: EXOBIOTANICA I-BOTANICAL SPACE FLIGHT” (2014), Black Rock Desert, Nevada. © AMKK
James Turrell, “Roden Crater” (2015). © James Turrell, © Skystone Foundation
Pannaphan Yodmanee, “In the aftermath” (2017-18), found objects, artist-made icons, plaster, resin, concrete, steel, pigment, dimensions variable. © Pannaphan Yodmanee, courtesy of Queensland Art Gallery Gallery of Modern Art
Lita Albuquerque, “Stellar Axis: Antarctica” (2006). Photo by Jean de Pomereu, courtesy of the artist and the Nevada Museum of Art. © Lita Albuquerque

title: In 'An American Fiction,' Ronald Jackson Casts an Imagined Screenplay
description: In the Oscar-winning film American Fiction, the irritable protagonist Thelonious “Monk” Ellison describes his work as follows: “I just invent litt
body:
In the Oscar-winning film American Fiction, the irritable protagonist Thelonious “Monk” Ellison describes his work as follows: “I just invent little people in my mind and make them have conversations with each other.” The film, which director Cord Jefferson adapted from Percival Everett’s novel Erasure, grapples with stereotypes and the ways we’re asked to perform our identities. For Monk, this turns into a satirical quest to write a “Black” book under a pen name, which plunges him into an outlandish world of tropes.
American Fiction layers farce upon farce and is one of the more searing considerations of the contemporary impulse to leverage identity for nefarious (and capitalist) purposes. In Monk’s world, “inventing little people” becomes a meta exercise that leads to more and more absurdity.
“Pervis Brown: The Apprentice of Oddly Uncommon Trades, played by Cornelius Dunston in AN AMERICAN FICTION” (2026), oil on canvas, 60 × 48 inches
The artist Ronald Jackson extrapolates the narrative further in his solo presentation opening this week at Galerie Myrtis. Known for his vibrant portraiture, Jackson creates a sort of casting list for an imagined screenplay that titles the exhibition: An American Fiction.
Through a suite of new oil paintings, the artist playfully envisions a troupe of figures, their names, and their roles. A portrait of a Black man with dreadlocks and red handkerchief tied around his neck, for example, is titled “Pervis Brown: The Apprentice of Oddly Uncommon Trades, played by Cornelius Dunston in AN AMERICAN FICTION.” All of the works are named in this vein, seeding the viewer’s understanding of the imaginary screenplay.
Jackson is familiar with this witty, cross-disciplinary approach. In an earlier body of work, he invented Johnnie Mae King, a recurring character for whom the artist invited the public to imagine a backstory through flash fiction and other writings. This figure also donned Jackson’s signature mask, which frequently appears in An American Fiction, too. He writes about the motif:

I use the mask not to conceal but to signal that a rich, un-excavated narrative exists beneath the surface. It asks the viewer to consider what lies beyond the visible role, prompting a question central to performance: are we admiring the superficial? Do we distinguish between the performer and the character being played? Do we recognize that there is likely a very different reality than the one being presented to us?

A playful, innovative approach to some of the most pressing questions in today’s culture, An American Fiction runs from September 5 to October 3 in Baltimore. Find more from Jackson on Instagram.
“Bradley ‘Ernesto’ Hillman with daughter Arlo: The Orchestrators of Unusual Happenings, played by Samuel Lead and Erica Dewberry in AN AMERICAN FICTION” (2026), oil on canvas, 72 × 60 inches
“Joy ‘Louise’ Parker: The Young Widow Who Returned Home, played by Regina Rhodes in AN AMERICAN FICTION” (2026) oil on canvas, 60 × 48 inches
“Sanford Billings: Shop Owner and Private Investigator, played by Malik Downs in AN AMERICAN FICTION” (2026), oil on canvas, 52 × 46 inches
“Greyman Dutch: Physician and Collector of Storied Relics, played by Dwight Jamesberry in AN AMERICAN FICTION” (2026), oil on canvas, 66 × 55 inches
“Barrett Dunnings: Jonesridge Cowboy and hired hand, played by Javon Campbell in AN AMERICAN FICTION” (2026) oil on canvas, 52 × 46 inches
“Abraham Jenkins: Rancher and town librarian, played by Dwight Jamesberry in AN AMERICAN FICTION” (2026), oil on canvas, 52 × 46 inches

description:

body:
Community
                “My studio is presently portable, modular, and itinerant.”
            
                
                                
                            
                
            
        
            Welcome to the 353rd installment of A View From the Easel, a series in which artists reflect on their workspace. This week, Rujuta Rao carries a foldable studio wherever she goes, a poetic embrace of her life between continents and mediums.Want to take part? Check out our submission guidelines and share a bit about your studio with us through this form! All mediums and workspaces are welcome, including your home studio.Rujuta Rao, New York CityHow long have you been working in this space?I've had this itinerant studio since January. I usually set it up in public spaces in New York City.Describe an average day in your studio.I tend to work on multiple projects in a circular manner, moving from one to another, working incrementally on each until I feel I've worked on them enough. I learned as a child that this way of working supports my swiftly moving attention and sustains my interest in each project. I work until 4am every day, and I enjoy talking to my family and friends in India while I work late. That is our time together.How does the space affect your work?My studio is presently portable, modular, and itinerant. I carry it around and set it up in public spaces. Each space and the people in it affect my work. The modular parts that compose my studio are also utilized in my performances and working with them in a studio context is a way to practice activating them in performance. The parts alternate between becoming work surfaces, bar-like interfaces to engage with people, and screens that create a sense of privacy in public.

title: LA’s Lucas Museum Displays “Narrative Art” for the Few, Not the People
description:
Feature

body:
Feature
                Friction, dissonance, and multiplicity are overall avoided in favor of superficial unity and a flattening of difference at George Lucas and Mellody Hobson's new institution.
            
                
                                
                            
                
            
                
        
            Mark Newman's "Padmé Fights Off Nexu" (2026) bronze statue in the garden of the Lucas Museum of Narrative Art (photo Chris Delmas/AFP via Getty Images; all other photos Matt Stromberg/Hyperallergic unless noted)
    
        
            LOS ANGELES — After nearly two decades of planning and construction, a spate of layoffs, and staffing controversies, the Lucas Museum of Narrative Art will open its doors to the public later this month in South Los Angeles’s Exposition Park. This week, members of the press were invited to tour the new institution and get a taste of the random and facile smorgasbord of art that awaits visitors. Founded by filmmaker George Lucas and his wife Mellody Hobson, co-CEO of Ariel Investments, the reportedly $1 billion building designed by Ma Yansong/MAD Architects houses their collection of 40,000 works representing what they call “visual storytelling.” These include illustrations, history paintings, comic art, films, murals, and other genres that “have not always received the respect they deserve,” as press materials explain. The five-story, undulating, spaceship-like structure sits on an 11-acre campus of rolling green hills designed by Mia Lehrer of Los Angeles’s Studio-MLA, who also designed the building’s green roof.A view of the Lucas Museum exterior“For thousands of years, that was the only way you could tell a story, with pictures,” Lucas said during a press preview on Wednesday, September 2 (seemingly disregarding traditions of oral histories or song). “Pictures and stories are very powerful. Put them together, and those two elements make a society.” “Narrative Art creates groups of people with common belief systems, which allows them to work together and not kill each other,” he continued, as if to finally resolve the question of what Narrative Art is, exactly, a query that has surrounded the museum for years.Ironically, there is very little narrative at all in the Museum of Narrative Art, at least curatorially. The collection is spread throughout 100,000 square feet of gallery space, divided into 30 or so thematic galleries — Adventure, Romance, Motherhood, Civic Life, Science Fiction, Comics, Sports, and others — with a few dedicated to individuals such as famed fantasy artist Frank Frazetta, American regionalist Thomas Hart Benton, and Norman Rockwell, whose specific brand of folksy Americana can be felt throughout. Artworks are displayed free of context or even any wall text aside from shiny, metal letters announcing each section. The thematic arrangement mashes together artworks of different styles and eras, linked by the flimsiest of threads, as if to say “Look, we’re all the same: we play sports, we work, we raise children!”, with little interest in exploring the specific cultural or social conditions from which they emerged.

title: Trump to Break Ground on “Triumphal Arch” Before Federal Approval
description:
News
                The announcement follows a series of recent rollbacks on federal protections of historically significant si
body:
News
                The announcement follows a series of recent rollbacks on federal protections of historically significant sites. 
            
                
                                
                            
                
            
                
        
            A model of the proposed "Great Triumphal Arch" displayed at the Great American State Fair on the National Mall in Washington, DC, United States, on July 2, 2026. (photo Nathan Posner/Anadolu via Getty Images)
    
        
            Excavation efforts are set to begin within the next two weeks for President Donald Trump’s controversial “Great Triumphal Arch,” according to a statement Interior Secretary Doug Burgum posted on X on Thursday, September 3. The announcement was made before the project has even received the green light from a federal review panel.The National Capital Planning Commission (NCPC), which evaluates design proposals throughout Washington, DC, preliminarily approved Trump's project on July 9, but issued several comments the president must address before earning the committee's final approval. The NCPC's primary concern is the height of the 250-foot-tall structure, which could violate the 130-foot cap imposed by the 1910 Height of Buildings Act and obstruct the sightlines of dozens of historical landmarks."This will be one of the Great Pieces of American Architecture, honoring the history and significance of Arlington Cemetery and befitting the most powerful Capital in the World," Burgum added in his post on Thursday, a month before the NCPC's next scheduled review on October 1.Sitting on the highly trafficked Memorial Circle near Arlington National Cemetery, the white granite-clad arch will include a “Military Observation Deck” and be topped by two statues of gold eagles and one of a golden winged figure. While the project has been presented as a celebratory marker of the country's 250th anniversary, Trump has also dedicated the monument, which many have deemed the “Arc de Trump,” to himself.
